newsitem.title: UK: Sinn Fein in talks with Ireland; Britain next.
newsitem.headline: Sinn Fein in talks with Ireland; Britain next.

text.p: The IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, ended months of international isolation on Saturday by holding talks with Irish officials and preparing for preliminary discussions with the new British government.

Sinn Fein President Gerry Adams and Vice-President Pat Doherty met Irish officials in Dublin for the first time since Prime Minister John Bruton's government banned contact after the Irish Republican Army (IRA) ended a 17-month truce last year.

The Dublin talks followed an initiative by Britain's new Prime Minister, Tony Blair, who on Friday said he would relax the ban on official contact with Sinn Fein without seeking an IRA ceasefire as a precondition.

Bruton said the goal of the talks was to seek a new ceasefire by the IRA to its 28-year guerrilla war against British rule of Northern Ireland, whose 60 per cent Protestant population want the province to stay British.
"We are not going to have meetings for the sake of meetings because that would compromise the safety of this state and its people," Bruton said in a statement.
"But if there is a genuine prospect of a ceasefire, a meeting can be organised to see if we can help bring that about."
Adams declined to give details of his discussions with Irish officials but said his office was in contact with the British government to arrange talks "without delay."
The Sinn Fein President and his chief negotiator, Martin McGuinness, travel to London on Monday after winning seats in the May 1 British elections.
But aides to the two said the talks were likely to take place in Northern ireland on Tuesday or Wednesday.
Adams played down expectations of a breakthrough on a ceasefire the IRA ended in February 1996 with a campaign which killed people in London and Northern Ireland.
He said the initiative by Blair was welcome but said much of the British Prime Minister's speech was tilted towards Protestant Unionists, who want the province to remain within Britain.

Blair told a Belfast audience that he had no intention of ending the 300-year-old Union between Britain and Northern Ireland and said he doubted whether the two Irelands would be reunited in his lifetime.
"I want to see the Union ended, not strengthened or modified," Adams told reporters in Newry, a border town.

Blair opened the door to preliminary talks with Sinn Fein providing there is no further IRA violence. There have been no IRA guerrilla attacks since a policewoman was shot and seriously injured in Londonderry last month.
British Defence Secretary, Gordon Robertson, visited Northern Ireland on Saturday for a briefing with army chiefs on the security situation.

Asked if he thought the IRA as observing an undeclared truce, Robertson told reporters: "I can't tell what their intentions are. There has been some cessation of some violence, but it is not enough," he said.
Adams said the talks with British officials were overdue because Sinn Fein was a legitimate political party which polled some 16 per cent of votes in the May 1 British election.

Blair said he would not invite Sinn Fein to Belfast peace talks until the IRA calls a permanent end to its war. But Adams said the IRA was "its own organisation. It can read all of this as well as anyone else."

Britain says Sinn Fein will continue to be barred from the talks, which group Unionists and Irish nationalists, because the IRA could try to sabotage any settlement it did not approve of unless it gave up violence altogether.
